title: Toto Wolff's journey from Williams to nine F1 titles
excerpt:
After guiding Mercedes to a ninth Constructors' Championship, Toto Wolff has drawn level with Sir Frank Williams in the history books. Here is how the Austrian became one of Formula 1's most successful team bosses.

When Mercedes secured their ninth Constructors' Championship at the 2026 Sao Paulo Grand Prix, it marked another significant milestone in the career of Team Principal Toto Wolff.

The result saw the Silver Arrows draw level with Williams on nine teams' titles, placing them behind only Ferrari and McLaren in Formula 1 history. For Wolff, the achievement carried particular significance given his beginnings in the sport.

Before overseeing Mercedes' record-breaking run of eight consecutive Constructors' Championships, the Austrian had made his first steps into Formula 1 management at Williams, working alongside the team's legendary founder, Sir Frank Williams.

Now, more than a decade after joining Mercedes, Wolff has matched Frank's tally of nine Constructors' titles, having guided the Brackley-based outfit back to the top following four seasons without championship success.

But how did a former racing driver and businessman become one of Formula 1's most successful team bosses?

A racing driver turned businessman

Born in Vienna in 1972, Wolff's motorsport career began behind the wheel rather than on the pit wall. After developing an interest in racing as a teenager, he competed in Austrian Formula Ford and claimed a class victory at the 1994 Nürburgring 24 Hours.

His racing career also included an appearance in the FIA GT Championship in 2004, although by this point, Wolff had already begun establishing himself in the business world, realising his talents lay beyond the cockpit.

He founded investment firms Marchfifteen in 1998 and Marchsixteen in 2004, with interests spanning technology and industrial businesses, while maintaining his connections to motorsport.

Those interests included HWA AG, the company responsible for Mercedes-Benz's DTM and Formula 3 programmes, providing Wolff with experience of the commercial and competitive sides of racing before entering Formula 1 management.

Finding his feet at Williams

Wolff's involvement in Formula 1 began in 2009 when he invested in Williams, a team already established as one of the most successful in the sport's history.

Founded by Sir Frank Williams and Sir Patrick Head, the outfit had won nine Constructors' Championships between 1980 and 1997, enjoying success with drivers including Nigel Mansell, Alain Prost, Damon Hill and Jacques Villeneuve.

Although Williams were no longer regularly challenging for titles when Wolff arrived, the Austrian developed a close relationship with Frank, eventually becoming the team's Executive Director in 2012.

Reflecting on their relationship in a 2020 interview with F1.com, Wolff recalled the moment they first met.

"Frank Williams is an incredible person, with an aura and charisma that very few people in Formula 1 possess. I was lucky enough to meet him personally in 2009, and I'll never forget the first thing he said to me: 'I heard you can help me repay my mortgage!'"

Wolff's time at Williams would prove relatively brief, however, as another opportunity emerged in 2013.

A new chapter with Mercedes

In February 2013, Wolff joined Mercedes as Managing Partner, acquiring a 30% stake in the Formula 1 operation and taking on wider responsibilities for the manufacturer's motorsport activities. The move placed him alongside three-time World Champion Niki Lauda and Team Principal Ross Brawn as Mercedes continued building towards the front of the grid.

Wolff's first season coincided with Lewis Hamilton arriving at Mercedes to join Nico Rosberg, beginning one of the most successful partnerships in the sport's history.

Mercedes secured three victories during the 2013 campaign, with Rosberg winning in Monaco and Great Britain before Hamilton took victory in Hungary. The team eventually finished second in the Constructors' Championship behind Red Bull.

However, the introduction of new turbo-hybrid power unit regulations in 2014 would transform the competitive order.

Mercedes won 16 of the season's 19 Grands Prix, while Hamilton secured his second Drivers' Championship after a season-long battle with Rosberg. The result also delivered the team's first Constructors' title.

It was the beginning of an unprecedented period of success.

Eight consecutive championships

Mercedes' dominance continued throughout the following seasons, as Wolff oversaw a team that established a new benchmark for consistency in Formula 1.

Hamilton added further Drivers' Championships in 2015, 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2020, while Rosberg defeated his childhood friend and team mate to claim the 2016 crown. And while despite the intense rivalry between their drivers, Mercedes maintained their position at the front, navigating regulation changes and challenges from Ferrari and Red Bull.

By 2021, the Silver Arrows had won eight consecutive Constructors' Championships, a record unmatched by any other Formula 1 team.

Although Hamilton narrowly missed out on an eighth Drivers' title to Max Verstappen that season, Mercedes secured another teams' crown, extending their extraordinary run of success.

A ninth title and a place alongside Frank Williams

Mercedes' remarkable winning streak ended in 2022, as the introduction of new ground effect regulations changed the competitive landscape and left the team struggling to match their rivals.

For Wolff, it marked the beginning of a challenging period, with Mercedes managing just five Grand Prix victories across the following four seasons. Despite the setbacks, the Austrian remained at the helm, overseeing changes to the team's driver line-up and preparations for another major regulation overhaul in 2026.

Hamilton's departure for Ferrari at the end of 2024 also marked the conclusion of one of Formula 1's most successful driver-team partnerships, with Wolff choosing to promote young Italian Kimi Antonelli alongside George Russell.

"I made up my mind five minutes after Lewis Hamilton told me that he's going to Ferrari," said Wolff following Antonelli's announcement in August 2024.

"That is the line-up with these two [Russell and Antonelli] that I always wanted, bearing in mind the fast-tracking that we did with Kimi and everything related there too, but that was immediately what I wanted to do."

The decision represented a significant show of faith in the then 18-year-old, who had progressed through Mercedes' junior programme before making his Formula 1 debut in 2025.

“Wolff's decision was vindicated in 2026, with Antonelli securing his maiden Drivers' Championship at the Mexico City Grand Prix, becoming the youngest World Champion in F1 history at just 20 years old.”

Mercedes' resurgence was completed at the following round in Sao Paulo, where Russell and Antonelli's fourth and fifth-place finishes secured the team's ninth Constructors' Championship, ending a four-year wait for another title.

The achievement marked Mercedes' ninth Constructors' Championship, their first since 2021, and brought Wolff level with Sir Frank Williams, whose nine titles had been won across the 1980s and 1990s.

Speaking to Sky Sports following the race, Wolff reflected on the significance of matching the man who had helped him establish his career in Formula 1.

"Obviously, Frank is such an unbelievable icon of the sport, and to be tied on constructors' championships, I never thought that was ever possible.

"I had a close relationship with Frank, and to be there, it's amazing. I can't believe it."

title: F1 ACADEMY Champion Palmowski graduates to Formula Regional
excerpt:
F1 ACADEMY Champion Alisha Palmowski will make the step up to the Formula Regional European Championship (FREC), with F1 ACADEMY and Red Bull Racing announcing she will receive a fully-funded seat with Rodin Motorsport for the 2027 season.

Additionally, the 20-year-old will join the Red Bull Junior Team next year and will benefit from a comprehensive testing programme, alongside continued support and development through the Red Bull Junior Programme and backing from F1 ACADEMY.

Palmowski made her debut in the all-female series in 2024 as a Wild Card driver for the penultimate round in Qatar. A successful appearance earned her a spot in the Red Bull Racing Academy Programme and a seat with Campos Racing for the 2025 campaign, going on to take victory in the opening race of the season in Shanghai.

After finishing fifth in the standings, the Briton returned for her sophomore campaign and a dominant run saw her crowned Champion last time out for the F1 ACADEMY's appearance in Austin.

Claiming five wins, seven podiums and six pole positions, Palmowski secured the title with three races remaining.

She becomes the third F1 ACADEMY Champion to progress up the single-seater ladder after Marta Garcia’s 2024 campaign in FREC and Abbi Pulling’s in the GB3 Championship.

Ahead of next season, Palmowski will also get behind the wheel for the 2027 Race of Champions New Zealand in January, partnering up with 13-time Formula 1 race winner David Coulthard as part of Team GB.

Susie Wolff, Managing Director of F1 ACADEMY, commented: “What a journey it’s been for Alisha. From joining us as a Wild Card Driver in 2024 to becoming F1 ACADEMY Champion just two years later, she has grabbed this opportunity with both hands. Not only has she proven herself a worthy Champion, but she has also demonstrated to Red Bull Racing that she warrants their continued support and a place in their Junior Programme.

Six defining moments on Palmowski's journey to becoming the 2026 F1 ACADEMY Champion

“Helping our Champions take the next step in their development is a part of our mission at F1 ACADEMY. We want to see them continue to progress and have the opportunities and support they need to climb further up the motorsport ladder.

“We are all proud of Alisha, not only for what she has achieved on track, but also for the character, determination and integrity she has shown off it. She is a fantastic role model for the next generation, and everyone at F1 ACADEMY will be cheering her on from afar as she takes on this next challenge.”

Alisha Palmowski, 2026 F1 ACADEMY Champion, added: “I’m so excited to continue my journey with the support of Red Bull and F1 ACADEMY behind me. Winning the F1 ACADEMY title in Austin, with my family there and so many people cheering me on, was surreal, and it’s a weekend I’ll never forget.

“I’ve developed so much as a driver and as a person over the last two seasons, and the support I’ve received from Campos Racing, Red Bull and F1 ACADEMY has been incredible. It’s taken a lot of hard work to get here, and I know there’s still a lot more to do but having that belief and support behind me makes the journey clearer.

“Next season brings a new series, a new team and a fresh opportunity to test myself. Moving up the single-seater ladder has always been the goal, and I’m incredibly grateful to have the opportunity to race in Formula Regional with Rodin Motorsport. I can’t wait to get going.”

title: Mercedes' incredible history of Formula 1 success
excerpt:
After Mercedes secured their ninth Constructors' Championship in 2026, F1.com looks back at the Silver Arrows' remarkable history, including Juan Manuel Fangio's early success, their record-breaking run of eight consecutive titles and their return to the top of Formula 1.

Mercedes have written their name into the F1 history books once again by clinching a ninth constructors' crown, their points at the 2026 Sao Paulo Grand Prix returning them to the top of the sport for the first time in five years.

George Russell and Kimi Antonelli's fourth and fifth-place finishes at Interlagos were enough to seal the teams' title, just one week after the young Italian claimed his maiden Drivers' Championship in Mexico.

The achievement puts Mercedes level with Williams on nine constructors' titles, behind only Ferrari's 16 and McLaren's 10, and adds another chapter to a remarkable history that stretches back more than seven decades.

Their success began on track long before Lewis Hamilton, Nico Rosberg and the modern Mercedes team won eight consecutive Constructors' Championships though, that period between 2014 and 2021 one of the most dominant in F1 history...

The Silver Arrows' early success

Mercedes' history in Grand Prix racing dates back well before the Formula 1 World Championship was established in 1950, with the famous Silver Arrows enjoying considerable success during the 1930s.

The German manufacturer made its World Championship debut at the 1954 French Grand Prix, with Juan Manuel Fangio and Karl Kling securing a one-two finish in their first race behind the wheel of the Mercedes W196.

Fangio went on to win four races for Mercedes that season, securing his second Drivers' Championship, before returning in 1955 to claim another title alongside team mate Stirling Moss. The following campaign saw Mercedes win five of the six World Championship Grands Prix in which they competed, including a famous victory for Moss at the British Grand Prix – the first of his 16 career wins.

However, Mercedes withdrew from motorsport at the end of 1955 following a season overshadowed by the Le Mans disaster, in which driver Pierre Levegh and more than 80 spectators lost their lives. The decision brought an early end to the manufacturer's first period of F1 success, with Mercedes having claimed two Drivers' Championships in just two seasons. The Constructors' Championship would not be introduced until 1958.

Mercedes eventually returned to F1 as an engine supplier during the 1990s, initially partnering with Sauber before beginning a successful relationship with McLaren, where drivers Mika Hakkinen and Lewis Hamilton would go on to win titles with Mercedes power.

But it would take until 2010 for the manufacturer to return to the grid as a full works team.

A new era of Mercedes dominance

After Brawn GP's remarkable championship-winning campaign in 2009, Mercedes purchased the Brackley-based outfit and returned to Formula 1 with seven-time World Champion Michael Schumacher and Nico Rosberg as their drivers.

The team's early seasons brought mixed results, although Rosberg secured Mercedes' first victory as a works team since 1955 at the 2012 Chinese Grand Prix.

The arrival of Hamilton in 2013 marked another significant moment, with the Briton joining Rosberg as Mercedes prepared for major changes to Formula 1's technical regulations.

When the turbo-hybrid era began in 2014, Mercedes emerged as the team to beat. Winning 16 of the season's 19 Grands Prix, Hamilton and Rosberg dominated the championship, with the former claiming his second drivers' title as Mercedes secured their first constructors' crown.

It was the beginning of an extraordinary run.

They repeated the feat in 2015, once again winning 16 of 19 races, before taking their dominance to another level in 2016, claiming 19 victories across 21 Grands Prix. That year also brought one of the sport's most memorable intra-team rivalries, with Rosberg defeating Hamilton to secure his maiden World Championship before announcing his retirement just days later.

Valtteri Bottas joined Mercedes for 2017, helping the team continue their winning streak alongside Hamilton, who added four consecutive drivers' titles between 2017 and 2020.

In their time together, Hamilton claimed six drivers' titles, Rosberg added another, and Mercedes established themselves as one of the most successful outfits the sport had ever seen.

Even when Max Verstappen ended their run of drivers' crowns in 2021, Mercedes maintained their advantage in the teams' standings.

By the end of that year, Mercedes had achieved something no other team in F1 history had managed – eight consecutive Constructors' Championships.

But major regulation changes in 2022 would bring an end to their reign.

Returning to the top in 2026

The introduction of new ground-effect regulations in 2022 proved challenging for Mercedes, who struggled to replicate their previous dominance.

Russell secured the team's only victory of that season in Sao Paulo, while 2023 marked their first winless campaign since 2011. And whilst the Silver Arrows returned to winning ways in 2024, claiming four victories, they finished fourth in the standings.

The departure of Hamilton to Ferrari at the end of that year also marked the conclusion of the most successful driver-team partnership in Formula 1 history, with the seven-time World Champion having secured 84 Grand Prix victories for Mercedes.

In his place came the then 18-year-old Italian Antonelli, who partnered Russell for the 2025 campaign. The team finished second in the standings that year, setting the stage for another major opportunity as the sport prepared to introduce new technical regulations for 2026.

Just as they had done in 2014, Mercedes capitalised on the changes.

Russell opened the 2026 season with victory in Australia, before Antonelli secured his maiden win in China and quickly established himself as a championship contender.

By the time the paddock arrived in Brazil, Mercedes had claimed 12 Grand Prix victories from 19 Grands Prix, with Antonelli having already secured the Drivers' Championship in Mexico.

Their ninth teams' title followed at Interlagos, completing another championship double and making Mercedes the third-most successful constructor in the sport's history, level with Williams.

For Team Principal Toto Wolff, who has overseen all nine of Mercedes' Constructors' Championships – an achievement that sees him equal Sir Frank Williams' record for the most titles as a team boss – the win carries particular significance after four challenging seasons.

"We've taken a few years to be back on the top spot. Not many teams have been able to come back from such a situation.

"And it just shows that, you know, the great work, the great people that we have in our organisation. And it's fantastic to be among them."

More than 70 years after Fangio first tasted championship success with Mercedes, the Silver Arrows have once again established themselves at the summit of Formula 1.

title: Why the F1 driver market might produce one last twist
excerpt:
On paper, the news Racing Bulls will keep both Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad for next season leaves just one spot to be confirmed, but there's still the possibility of a change in one other seat on the grid...

So what's up for grabs in that one spot yet to be confirmed?

A seat at American squad Haas. Ollie Bearman is the incumbent and is going to be in it next year – they just haven't nailed down the details of the contract.

The Briton and Ferrari junior is in his second full season with Haas and currently sits in 13th place in the drivers' standings on 23 points.

He's levelled up in his second campaign, both in terms of Qualifying pace and racecraft – with the 21-year-old pulling off some particularly impressive overtakes.

Haas certainly want to keep him – so it's just a case of his management, Haas boss Ayao Komatsu and Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur coming to an agreement.

While it is a no-brainer for all parties to continue, the terms of the deal are important as Bearman will know that if Lewis Hamilton keeps delivering, he won't be leaving Ferrari anytime soon and that means there's no space for the Briton to move up.

And while Haas is a great place to be for Bearman for now – and his full focus is taking the team forward and helping them achieve the first podium in their history – he also knows he can't stay there forever if he wants to progress his career.

Watch this space, but it's certainly a case of when, not if, a deal is done for 2027.

'We see huge potential' – Komatsu on choosing Camara for Haas

Okay, that finalises the grid – so what's this about a possible change?

Well, this is where we turn our attention to Cadillac. When Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas signed with the newcomers ahead of this campaign, they both agreed multi-year deals.

These multi-year deals had options which needed triggering to confirm the second season in 2027.

Ahead of the Mexico City Grand Prix, Cadillac announced Perez had signed an extended deal keeping him at the team until at least the end of 2029.

A subsequent announcement about Bottas has yet to be released, with the team's American reserve driver Colton Herta linked with the seat that would offer him his F1 debut.

Herta has struggled in F2 and sits 19th in the standings, but the 26-year-old has impressed when behind the wheel of a Cadillac in FP1 sessions and the American team are keen to run an American driver on merit.

By taking part in the opening practice session in Brazil, Herta secured the final point needed for his Super Licence, clearing the way for a potential F1 drive.

Cadillac now have to decide whether they want to give him a debut next year or stick with 37-year-old 10-time Grand Prix winner Bottas alongside Perez.

What about one-time Grand Prix winner Esteban Ocon?

Given Haas are set to sign Bearman and Cadillac will have Bottas or Herta, it means there is no space on the grid for Ocon, who made his F1 debut back in 2016.

Earlier this month, Haas announced that Ocon would not complete the season with the team, which he was set to leave at the end of the year anyway.

Ocon – who has won one Grand Prix, taken four podiums and scored 490 points in 198 starts – has unfinished business with F1 and wants to find a way back in.

Initially, that will have to be a reserve role at best and with his experience in F1, it's believed he does have options for 2027.

title: Tsolov to serve as Red Bull and Racing Bulls reserve driver
excerpt:
Red Bull and Racing Bulls have confirmed that Formula 2 racer Nikola Tsolov will serve as their shared reserve driver for the 2027 season.

The announcement follows the news that Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad will continue to form Racing Bulls’ driver line-up for another year, ending speculation that Tsolov could be promoted to a full-time seat.

Instead, the Bulgarian will join both the Faenza-based outfit and sister team Red Bull in a reserve capacity, which means he will be on standby to race if required, develop the car through simulator work, and get the opportunity to drive in further FP1 sessions – having previously impressed during his first outing in Mexico City – and Testing of Previous Cars (TPC).

The move follows Tsolov's progression through the junior categories, having finished runner-up in the 2025 Formula 3 championship before stepping up to F2, where he remains in title contention with two rounds remaining.

Tsolov said: “I’m incredibly happy and grateful to Red Bull for giving me this opportunity. Since joining the Junior Team, I’ve received amazing support and have developed so much, both as a driver and as a person. My career has progressed incredibly quickly, and I owe a lot to everyone who has believed in me and helped me get to this point.

“My ambition is clear: I want to become an F1 driver. Having the opportunity to spend next year preparing for that next step is incredibly exciting.

“I’m confident that with the Team’s support and experience, I’ll have the best possible preparation to make sure I’m fully ready to take the next step onto the F1 grid when the time comes.

“I know there is still a lot to learn, but I’m ready to work hard, make the most of every opportunity and give everything I have to the Team. For now, my immediate focus is on finishing the F2 season as strongly as possible.”

CEO and Red Bull Team Principal Laurent Mekies added: “Nikola is an exceptionally talented young driver, and we have been hugely impressed by his development and performances over the past few years.

“To fight for the Championship in F3 and now challenge for the F2 title in his first full season says a great deal about his ability and determination. What has impressed us just as much is his maturity, his approach to racing and his willingness to keep learning and improving.

“We have enormous belief in Nikola’s potential and see him as a driver with a very exciting future in F1. This appointment reflects our confidence in him and our commitment to his continued development. Our focus in 2027 will be on giving him the experience, tools and support he needs to be ready to race in F1 next.

“For now, Nikola still has an important job to finish in F2. We wish him every success in the final two rounds and will be supporting him all the way as he fights for the Championship.”

title: Russell launches new karting academy for young racers
excerpt:
George Russell has revealed the creation of his own karting academy, which will seek to find “hidden stars” and provide support to help them progress in motorsport when it officially launches in 2027.

The Mercedes driver teased the announcement earlier this week as he praised karting for teaching him “the fundamentals of racing” and making him the competitor he is now, adding his ambition to “give back to a sport that gave me so much”.

The GR63 Academy will begin with open-access qualifiers at Silverstone in December, with 80 young drivers progressing to a shoot-out before 25 are selected for the 2027 championship.

“So proud to introduce you all to the GR63 Academy,” Russell shared on social media. “Karting is where it all started for me and has played a crucial role in my career. I also know how hard it is for talented young drivers to get that first opportunity, especially when budgets are tight.

“With the GR63 Academy, I want to give something back to my sport by finding those hidden stars and giving them the support and guidance they need to reach their potential.

“Following the first two rounds at Silverstone, I’ll identify 25 kids to take part in the GR63 Academy in 2027. Thank you to Silverstone and the BRDC for helping make this happen.”

The academy's official website outlines the selection process, beginning with Arrive & Drive Qualifiers in December. Children aged eight or nine can participate for £25 per qualifying session.

The 80 fastest drivers will advance to a shoot-out at the end of January, with 25 selected to compete in the GR63 Championship – a fully funded, eight-round series held across different circuit configurations at Kart Silverstone.

Equipped with a full set of Russell’s signature vibrant blue kit, they will battle to finish in the top five, which will earn them a spot in the final shoot-out. There, the remaining youngsters will be assessed on “talent, lap times, fitness, race craft and media skills”, with the winner receiving a fully-funded kart season in 2028.

Russell believes the initiative could help uncover F1's next generation of talent by providing a more accessible route into competitive karting.

“That commitment has played a big part in Britain’s long record of success in motorsport, and it is a great source of pride for the Club and its Members.

title: Why Racing Bulls stuck with Lawson and Lindblad
excerpt:
There'll be no change in Racing Bulls' line-up for next season, with Arvid Lindblad's encouraging rookie year and a sensational campaign from Liam Lawson enough to secure their respective seats.

Why did Lindblad get the nod?

Lindblad has caught the eye this year, kicking off life in F1 with points on debut in Australia and going on a run of 10 points finishes in 11 Grands Prix weekends midway through the year.

His progression both on and off track has been solid through the year, with the team impressed with his feedback, calmness under pressure and natural speed.

Though the last four events have been point-less for the 19-year-old, there was still underlying growth in his performances, including a strong drive from 18th to 11th last time out in Brazil.

It's believed that Red Bull and Racing Bulls have been convinced for some time that Lindblad, who sits 11th in the Drivers' Standings, deserved another year.

What was the challenge with the second seat?

The second seat was less certain because even if Lawson was enjoying the best season of his career by quite some distance, Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov was making waves in F2.

Lawson has looked like a driver reborn at Racing Bulls, following his demotion from Red Bull after just two races at the start of 2025, with his performance in 2026 particularly impressive.

The 24-year-old has scored points in 15 of the 20 Grands Prix this year (two of those were when he subbed in at Red Bull) - as well as taking points in three Sprints where only the top eight score.

That form puts him best of the rest and top of the midfield pack in P9 in the drivers' standings with a points tally of 89, more than double the tally of the next best driver Pierre Gasly.

However, with Tsolov leading the championship in F2 until the previous round when he was usurped by Ferrari junior and incoming full-time Haas driver Rafa Camara, Red Bull were considering promoting him.

With six victories in F2, Tsolov has well and truly been one to watch, and when he got behind the wheel of the Racing Bulls machine in FP1 at Mexico, he impressed the team with his speed and feedback.

Lawson and Lindblad to remain at Racing Bulls for 2027

That piled pressure on Lawson. Despite impressing during his three-race stint replacing the injured Isack Hadjar at Red Bull, a permanent return appears unlikely, strengthening the case for Racing Bulls to develop another potential Red Bull driver.

Racing Bulls Team Principal Alan Permane, who was recently handed a new contract that will keep him at the helm until at least the end of 2031, told me last year that he wants the team to be "an incubator for talent".

And so that's why Racing Bulls found themselves with a dilemma.

Why did they choose Lawson over Tsolov?

Ultimately, it came down to performance. Lawson's tally of 89 points has been crucial in the team establishing themselves in P5 in the Teams' Championship, 45 points clear of Alpine.

The Faenza-based team have never finished as high as fifth in their 20-year history, so Lawson's contribution to putting them on the path to making history played a big role.

Even with the pressure of Tsolov waiting in the wings, Lawson has absorbed it all and continued to deliver across the last triple header, following a ninth in Austin with a brace of seventh places.

That form - combined with his results across the rest of the year - is what Red Bull and Racing Bulls will have hoped to get from a driver in one of their cars.

His race craft has tightened up, he's cut out the mistakes - and he seems to have found a way to get the best out of himself more consistently across a race weekend.

The New Zealander works well with Lindblad and they felt that continuity and stability was the right move for 2027 as they look to build on their very strong campaign in 2026.

What does that mean for Tsolov?

The Bulgarian will have to wait a little longer, but it's believed it's a case of when, not if, he'll make the step up to Formula 1 with the Red Bull family.

The energy drinks firm rate him highly and he's progressing as they would expect. Having more time to prepare himself for a debut in Formula 1 can only be a good thing.

The team haven't confirmed what his role will look like going forward but it's likely they will make him a reserve driver to continue his integration with the team.

It's also likely that he will get more opportunities in FP1 - teams have to run a rookie in at least four FP1s per year - and some running in old-spec F1 machinery to continue to build his experience.

All this puts Racing Bulls in a very strong position. They have two drivers performing at a very high level and one driver readying himself for a step up.

It's exactly how they and Red Bull will have hoped their junior programme conveyor belt would work.

title: Lawson and Lindblad to remain at Racing Bulls for 2027
excerpt:
Racing Bulls have confirmed they will field an unchanged line-up of Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad for the 2027 season, with both drivers extending their contracts with the team.

Lawson’s future at Racing Bulls has been the subject of speculation in recent months, with Red Bull Junior Nikola Tsolov emerging as a potential replacement and Team Principal Alan Permane repeatedly insisting that no final decision had been made.

Speaking a week after Tsolov made his FP1 debut for Racing Bulls, Permane explained that the team were “trying to apply a little bit of science” to make “the right decision”.

That has led to the New Zealander’s new deal, which also comes after his spectacular Sao Paulo Grand Prix weekend where he started third and wound up seventh, taking him to 89 points in the standings – more than the season total for Racing Bulls’ midfield rivals Alpine.

It marked his fourth seventh-place finish in five Grands Prix and strengthened Racing Bulls' grip on fifth in the Constructors' Championship. Should they retain that position, it would represent their best-ever result, dating back to their origins as Minardi.

Additionally, Lawson's team mate Lindblad has contributed a crucial 38 points to that goal and impressed with his consistency as a rookie, earning a sophomore campaign with Racing Bulls.

Lawson said: “I’m very happy to be continuing with Visa Cash App Racing Bulls next year. We’ve had a brilliant season together and the team has worked very hard to produce a fast car, which I’ve loved driving.

"It feels great to be part of a historic season for the team as we continue our fight for P5 in the Constructors' Championship. It's a testament to the hard work of everyone both at track, and back at the factory.

"I’m looking forward to carrying this moment forward with Arvid through to 2027; we’re building something super positive and I’m excited by what we can achieve together.”

Lindblad added: "I'm very happy to be continuing with Visa Cash App Racing Bulls in 2027. Looking back on my first season in Formula One, it's been a truly special year, full of new experiences and learnings since the very first pre-season test.

"I'd like to thank everyone at VCARB and Red Bull for their trust and support. I'm incredibly grateful to everyone in the team for their hard work, commitment and collaboration throughout the season, and for the strong relationships we've built along the way.

"I can't wait to get started next year, building on everything I've learned during my rookie season. It's set to be an exciting year, and I look forward to continuing to drive alongside Liam."

Team Principal Permane said: "We’re delighted to be continuing with Liam and Arvid for 2027. Both have demonstrated their ability and potential throughout the season, and we’ve seen the progress they’ve made, both individually and as a pairing.

"I have no doubt that this is the best driver line-up for us, bringing a strong combination of experience and ambition. Together, we have a solid foundation to build on the progress made this year, continue pushing ourselves forward and take the next step towards achieving our ambitions in 2027."

The announcement leaves two uncertainties on the 2027 grid, with Haas yet to disclose news of a contract for Ollie Bearman, although both parties have expressed a desire to continue working together.

Over at Cadillac, Valtteri Bottas was signed to a multi-year deal, but an extension for his team mate Sergio Perez – as well as the completed mission to secure a Super Licence for test driver Colton Herta – have raised some question marks around his place on the grid next season.

title: Ricciardo reacts to his best career moments
excerpt:
Daniel Ricciardo brought an energy to F1 that the sport had never quite witnessed before, adding a sense of joy and humour that delighted both those in the paddock and at home. But more importantly, he was a determined, ruthless competitor who clinched eight Grand Prix victories across stints at Red Bull and McLaren.

Two years have passed since the Australian left the sport, so he recently took the time to relive his greatest highlights and offer unprecedented insight into his career in an exclusive interview…

Ricciardo’s first victory

In his first season with Red Bull, Ricciardo had stood on the podium twice before securing his maiden victory at the 2014 Canadian Grand Prix. Starting from sixth on the grid, he steadily worked his way up and benefitted from Lewis Hamilton’s retirement to bring himself into contention in the race’s final stages.

Decisive moves on Sergio Perez and Nico Rosberg over the last few laps sealed the win for Ricciardo, and all he could get out over the radio was a chuckle and “wow!”.

“I didn't really know what to say,” he explained. “I think it was such a young laugh of shock and joy. I mean, the first emotion is – I don't know, is nostalgia an emotion? It feels so familiar, but also so long ago. I'm also just very grateful to have been able to experience this feeling. That's the highest high in the sport. Beyond that is to win a World Championship.

“For many years, I didn't feel like my career was a success because the World Championship was something that I was so fixed on and believed in. But I think now looking back, I'm like, okay, this was pretty awesome to still be able to get these moments.”

When his maiden pole position led to heartbreak in Monaco

Ricciardo already had three victories under his belt when he took his long-awaited maiden pole position and established himself as something of a Monaco specialist.

“That was a good lap,” he summarised. “I remember that. That was a good car as well. Monaco is special. There was definitely a good chunk of my career that I felt like I had an edge in Monaco.

“I had two poles in three years there. It didn't feel like a big deal because I was so high on confidence and that belief in myself – not in an arrogant way, just it didn't even feel like a big deal. It was like, yeah, this is my track.

“I was an intense young human being. [There was a] certain period of time where I felt untouchable on those streets. I just felt like I was willing to take more risks and I was very happy to get my first pole, but I was nearly angry that I hadn't got it sooner. That's why I was like, now it's my time. I was running very high on confidence.

The F1 drivers who waited longest for a first pole position

“I couldn't do that today, but I can still take myself there and remember the feeling. I know why I was able to do it. Sometimes it does feel a little bit out of body. I think in those moments, maybe I was someone else.”

After beating Mercedes to the top spot around the Monte Carlo streets, he led the race in wet conditions and opted for a different strategy to Hamilton, switching from full wet tyres, to intermediates, and finally to slicks.

But when he peeled into the pits for his final stop, the Red Bull crew were equipped with the wrong compound, forcing Ricciardo to wait whilst they scrambled for the correct tyres. That allowed Hamilton to demote him to P2, and despite his best efforts to regain first place, he finished 7.252s behind the Briton.

“I left hardly anything on the table,” Ricciardo admitted. “There were certainly some years there that I didn't have that level of confidence and it went from being the best track for me to one of the worst, just like that.

“I think at the end of the day, what it was is they reacted to Lewis and what he did. I think they changed at the last second what to do. In simple terms, it's like they forgot the basics – control your controllables. I think there was panic and it was a mess. That was definitely one of my worst days in F1. I think if I never won Monaco after that, it would still hurt me a lot more.”

Redemption in Monaco

Two seasons later, Ricciardo took the Monaco win he deserved, albeit not in the most straightforward of ways. He had the advantage of starting from pole, but suffered a power loss for the majority of the 2018 event that made holding off Sebastian Vettel even more difficult.

“I had a very wounded car,” he explained. “At that moment, some of my lack of knowledge with the way Formula 1 cars work and how an engine works and those hybrid engines and all of this… I didn't really know what the problem was. I probably should have known, but if I knew, I think it would have made me realise how much worse it was.

“F1 cars have eight gears. In Monaco, because it's a shorter straight, you don't really even get to eight. So you're already just using seven gears. With that problem, I was only using six, so I had so much less power.

“I was telling the team and they were just giving me instructions like move your brakes forward or do this or do that. It was just problem solving. They weren't really giving me the script on what the problem was.”

While Ricciardo’s triumph overshadowed the painful memories from 2016 – and led to his iconic celebration in the Red Bull swimming pool – it came at the end of a day filled with anxiety and dread for the Australian.

He said: “I don't have 100 wins. I had eight, so they're all very special. But yes, more was on that than 2016. I think getting another chance to win Monaco made the pressure even higher.

“I just wanted it to be over. I wasn't looking forward to the race. I wasn't excited about anything. I was just like, I've hardly slept. Everyone's coming up to me, wishing me luck and trying to give me advice. I just want to go hide and get this race done and hopefully win and then go drink!

“The drivers that had won in Monaco that had raced with Red Bull had done flips into the pool. I was like, look, I'm probably going to embarrass myself. It's already been done. What's something that feels me? What feels kind of goofy? One of my favourite movies is Me, Myself and Irene. I love Jim Carrey.

“There's a scene where he leaps off a bridge and I feel like the way I did it, it was my memory of how he did it in that film. I was like, this will feel silly. I'm kind of laughing at myself doing a belly flop. A bit like the shoey, I didn't think it would be that cool at the time and it ended up being probably the most beautiful thing ever in F1!”

It became just as memorable as his shoey celebration, which involved drinking champagne out of his race boot to “show Australia that I'm proud to be Australian”. Other drivers and celebrities were convinced to join in, including Hamilton, Max Verstappen and acclaimed actor Sir Patrick Stewart.

“There was definitely a conscious part of it where the sport was still very serious,” Ricciardo described. “I would sometimes see drivers on the podium and they looked kind of miserable, and I couldn't really understand why. I get it if you lose the race on the last lap and you finish second instead of first, but there's just a lot of situations where I was like, the sport feels a little stiff.

“That was also my way of trying to bring in something else to the sport. It felt like the tie was choking everyone, and I was like, let's just undo a button here and relax a little. Then it just became my thing.

“I weirdly became relatable through doing the silly things. I realised it made it more fun for everyone else around me. Look, you have to get results to back it up. There was a time and place still, but I felt like the team appreciated it. I know it's serious and there's a lot of money and business involved in the sport, but we can still make it fun.”

Returning to glory with McLaren

Having left Red Bull in 2018, Ricciardo went on to race for Renault and McLaren, claiming his final race win with the latter at the 2021 Italian Grand Prix. After passing his former team mate Verstappen at the start, he beat Lando Norris to give the Woking-based outfit their first victory in nine years.

“I remember hearing the team in the background all celebrating and losing their minds, so that made me really happy,” he concluded. “When you succeed in the sport, everyone in the team feels a part of it. To celebrate it with such a big group of people, it's like a party.

“[It was] a year that I questioned myself a lot and lacked a lot of confidence – I hadn’t won in a few years, and I questioned, will I ever win again? That was a very real question. When it's been so long, you start having doubts as a team and as an organisation.

“For all of us to feel this sense of relief and like, oh my gosh, we do belong here. I knew it was our best chance of getting a podium that year, or my best chance, because I knew the car. We were quick on the straights, and Monza is very much a straight-line circuit.

Ranking Ricciardo’s 8 Grand Prix wins

“I always felt really good in Monza. It was a track I enjoyed, and I felt like myself again. I just had a certain mindset, which brought out a certain inner confidence. Was I thinking [I could] win? No, I was thinking a podium.

“It was my first win with another team, so that was also something I was personally proud of. Probably two months before that, I was very low, extremely low. I was proud of myself to be able to find it within me to pull it off.

“The opposite side of success can feel very lonely, but everyone played a part in winning on that day. Pit stop, strategy, reliability – it all just worked and everyone knows that they did their bit and they helped get that car to cross the line first. Celebrating with the team and seeing everyone smile as big as your own, that's very cool.”

title: F1 drivers voice dissent after major test despite George Russell optimism
excerpt:
F1 drivers have delivered a definitive verdict against Pirelli's wet-weather tyres following their first major use in 2026.

During the Sao Paulo GP weekend, qualifying was held in dreadfully wet conditions, which necessitated the use of the extreme full wet tyres in competition for the first time this season, with Sunday's grand prix running wet-dry-wet, with the intermediate tyres being given a proper run-out for the first time.

The grand prix was the first time this season that a grand prix had started in wet conditions, and drivers were forced to change from slicks to the intermediates during a race, with the late shower in the closing laps.

The intermediate tyres had been used in both Bahrain in Malaysia and in the Singapore Sprint, but track conditions, aided by high track temperatures, quickly allowed the surfaces to dry and drivers to swap for slicks in Sepang, whilst they nursed the intermediates home in the Saturday race at Marina Bay.

Although Pirelli has been able to conduct specialised wet weather testing throughout 2026, including via Racing Bulls at Suzuka and Lewis Hamilton for Ferrari at Fiorano, the wet-weather tyres remain tricky to design.

In previous years, the full wet tyre was almost eradicated as a choice owing to its poor design, compounded by the fact that tyre blankets were not allowed to pre-heat them on cost and environmental grounds - but a call from Hamilton, in part, helped to ease the ban.

Reflecting, Mercedes driver Russell felt the Sao Paulo weekend and first major competition use of the intermediates and full wets had gone well.

"It has been substantially better than we all anticipated," Russell told media, including RacingNews365.

"I think it is also important to realise that the three tracks we've driven on have been very rough tarmac, and Malaysia and the Singapore Sprint were still hot, even in the rain.

"In [Sao Paulo qualifying], even though it was raining, the track was 30 degrees, but maybe, in the 15 degrees of Spa, we're giving different feedback."

However, Russell's fellow GPDA director Carlos Sainz counteracted that claim.

"Not good enough," said Sainz when asked for his feedback.

"I think the level of the inter and the wet tyre is not good enough, and we need to work with Pirelli on finding a better tyre, because in the mixed conditions, the inter is still a very weak tyre at the rear.

"By the time it warms up, the front is gone, and for the extreme wets, [in qualifying] we had much aquaplaning and a big lack of rear grip.

"So it is still missing a bit of development on these two tyres."

[Article continues below]

Fascinating insight into ongoing battle

Sainz's Williams team-mate Alex Albon then offered a fascinating insight into the battle drivers are facing to fire the intermediate and wet tyres up to allow them to operate in a suitable working window.

"I think the inter and the wet tyre isn't working very well at the moment," he said, after describing the wet tyre as "really poor" and the intermediate as "semi-sensible" following qualifying.

"I don't think it is the cars; it is the tyres, and we need to figure it out because the laps to the grid [prior to the São Paulo GP] were insane, really insane.

"I couldn't believe how little grip there was, and then the wet tyre overheats immediately, so we do need to make a better wet tyre for next year.

"What we've done with the power reduction and all that kind of stuff, we kind of need at the minute, and maybe if we had grippier inter and wet tyres, we'd be able to run at 350kw, but it is sketchy.

"It is difficult to fire the tyres up, but they also wear quite quickly, so even when they are cold, they're wearing.

"It feels like they never overheat or get up to temperature, and then by the time you are circulating, the tread is already coming off the tyre, and then you're struggling.

"You're sliding around, so you never feel good at any point, and feel that we can come to life."

title: Lando Norris 'master' trait singled out after stunning tour de force
excerpt:
Lando Norris's "master" ability to accurately read track conditions and his "sensitivity" in adapting to them have been highlighted by McLaren boss Andrea Stella.

Outgoing world champion Norris returned to winning ways in the Sao Paulo Grand Prix with a masterful performance in the wet-dry-wet race at Interlagos, where he won by 14 seconds in a dominant performance.

The Briton had also claimed pole position by two-tenths over George Russell in Saturday's dreadfully wet qualifying session, delayed by almost 90 minutes due to the rain.

Stella has spoken previously of Norris holding a "superpower" in low-grip conditions and excelling as he finds pace, with the 2025 champion particularly strong in the wet.

Reflecting after Norris's third win of the season, Stella said he believed the "master" Norris was ahead of his time in using the skills available to constantly adapt to the conditions underneath him.

"When Lando operates at his best, he's definitely one of the best drivers on the grid, and we have seen that in these [wet] conditions," Stella told media, including RacingNews365.

"It is not the first time that when you have mixed variable conditions, he is one of the fastest in finding the limit - and when the track was in the middle of dry and wet, he was probably gaining more [time] throughout the race than anybody.

"So I think he's very sensitive in understanding how much grip is available and very, I would say, even complete as a driver, despite still having many years ahead of him from a technical point of view in terms of understanding how to deploy his tools to use the grip that is available or to adapt to the balance of the car.

"Because you're never going to have a real, really perfect car. You're never going to have the perfect conditions. So adaptability is actually probably the most important feature that you want to possess as a driver.

"I think that's one that should be definitely acknowledged and recognised for Lando when there's a need to understand what's best and how to operate. He is definitely a master."

[Article continues below]

Stella's hope

Both Norris and team-mate Oscar Piastri have expressed how difficult the MCL40 machine is to drive and to extract performance from.

Adding to his comments, Stella expressed his wish for the car to be made more user-friendly.

"Hopefully, let me say, we don't need to rely on these qualities," he said of Norris's adaptability.

"We just want to make sure that we can offer Lando and Oscar a competitive car such that they can just drive a little bit more easily because our car still remains pretty difficult."

title: Electrifying Max Verstappen eerily foreshadows stunning F1 streak
excerpt:
A decade ago, Max Verstappen showed all the signs of things to come, with a masterful performance at Interlagos that he has already replicated three times and counting.

Ten years ago today, Max Verstappen produced a drive at Interlagos that would turn out to be less a one-off miracle than a preview of a pattern now stretching across the past three São Paulo Grands Prix.

On 13 November 2016, Verstappen's Red Bull speared sideways down the start-finish straight at well over 300km/h, snapping into a half-spin that threatened to send him into the barriers.

He somehow gathered it up, kept the car pointing forward, and did not lose a place to Nico Rosberg in the process.

"My heartbeat went a bit higher there!" he radioed to his engineers afterwards, a line that undersold the moment by some distance.

That save was merely the prelude. Verstappen had started fourth but been shuffled down the order as Red Bull gambled on strategy, switching him to intermediates in a bid to jump Lewis Hamilton for the win. The rain kept falling, the gamble failed, and the team was forced to pit again for extreme wets.

The Dutchman, then just 19, dropped outside the top ten and eventually as low as P16 with 16 laps still to run.

[Article continues below]

Driver

Max Verstappen

3

A charge through the spray

What followed was a wet-weather masterclass that has aged remarkably well. Running fresh rubber while those ahead nursed worn tyres, Verstappen darted off the traditional racing line, hunting grip in puddles and dirty air where rivals dared not venture, and scythed past car after car in near-zero visibility.

He charged from P16 to third, claiming the fastest lap along the way, and crossed the line behind only the two Mercedes of Hamilton and Rosberg.

"I had a massive moment, locked all four wheels, and managed to keep it out of the guardrail and continue still in second," Verstappen said afterwards, reflecting on the spin that so nearly ended his afternoon before the real drama had even begun.

"At the end, when I crossed the line, it felt like a victory; it was almost as beautiful as the race I had in Barcelona," he added, referencing his maiden win for Red Bull earlier that season.

Red Bull boss Christian Horner had no hesitation in rating it among the very best he had witnessed.

"His recovery was amazing, and that was one of the best drives I've seen in Formula One. We gave him a huge amount to do, and the way he drove those last 15 laps was unbelievable."

Mercedes' own hierarchy were equally struck. Non-executive chairman Niki Lauda admitted he had never seen anything quite like it, while Toto Wolff, watching a rival somehow upstage his own one-two, joked that the laws of physics were being rewritten in real time.

"The Verstappen show! It was really unbelievable driving, great entertainment. Physics are being redefined," Wolff said.

[Article continues below]

The pattern repeats

What makes 13 November 2016 more than a nostalgic footnote is what has followed at the same venue since.

In 2024, Verstappen won from P17 on the grid in wet conditions, prompting Horner to again reach for the word masterclass.

In 2025, he carved from the pit lane to third. And at the 2026 São Paulo Grand Prix just days ago, he climbed from P21 to finish second behind Lando Norris, continuing an extraordinary run of Interlagos recoveries that now spans a decade.

Pundits have repeatedly reached for the same historical comparisons each time it happens.

Karun Chandhok likened the recurring theme to Ayrton Senna's Donington masterclass of 1993 and Michael Schumacher's wet-weather dominance in Spain in 1996, drivers who did not merely want to win but to leave a mark.

Martin Brundle, reflecting on the 2025 edition, called it a drive for the ages built on sheer pace rather than circumstance alone.

Whether it is freak weather, Red Bull's setup suiting the bumpy Interlagos tarmac, or simply a driver who finds grip where nobody else can, the debate continues. But the pattern first laid down on that sodden afternoon in 2016 has proven anything but a coincidence.

title: Adrian Newey makes important claim about Aston Martin and 'disappointed' Honda
excerpt:
Honda has a winning history in F1, from its stints with McLaren and Red Bull. However, its early partnership with Aston Martin has fallen well short of expectations.

Adrian Newey has stressed that Aston Martin and Honda must focus on their F1 future together after admitting the Japanese manufacturer has been disappointed by its lack of progress this season.

The two companies joined forces as works partners for 2026, but their first campaign together has fallen far short of expectations, with Honda's power unit struggling for both performance and reliability.

Severe vibrations and battery failures disrupted pre-season preparations and the opening races, leaving Aston Martin short of mileage as it attempted to develop its new car.

Despite subsequent improvements, the Japanese marque has been unable to close the performance deficit to its rivals as quickly as hoped.

"I think it's fair to say that Honda have probably been a little bit disappointed with how much progress they have managed to make this year," Newey told media, including RacingNews365.

"But as always, or as is so often the case in that situation, it only strengthens resolve to go forward in the future."

[Article continues below]

The 'important bit' for Aston Martin and Honda

Aston Martin sits P10 in the constructors' standings on just seven points after 20 rounds, ahead only of newcomer Cadillac.

All seven have been scored by Fernando Alonso, who finished P10 in Monaco, ninth in the Netherlands and eighth at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. Team-mate Lance Stroll remains without a point.

Honda has introduced engine and turbo upgrades during the campaign, as part of the FIA's additional development and upgrade opportunities (ADUO) programme, but those have not delivered the breakthrough needed to lift Aston Martin into regular points contention.

Nevertheless, Newey believes the foundations are being put in place for a stronger future, although he acknowledged that a turnaround would take time.

"I think the future is obviously the important bit for both companies," Newey added. "As I've mentioned before, they are very determined.

"These things don't change overnight, but they have a lot of good people and a lot of good processes now in place."

title: Dan Ticktum explains how Fortescue beat Lola to his Formula E signature
excerpt:
Dan Ticktum has a new home for the start of Formula E's Gen4 era, but just how did it come about?

13 November 10:20AM

Dan Ticktum has detailed how a meeting with Gary Ekerold months before his Formula E future was decided played a decisive role in him joining Fortescue Zero Racing for the new Australian-owned outfit's debut season.

Ticktum left Cupra Kiro at the end of the previous campaign and was widely linked with Fusion, the new customer squad built around Porsche's Gen4 powertrains after the German manufacturer scrapped plans for an in-house second factory team.

Ticktum also undertook testing with Lola Yamaha and held a contract offer from the Silverstone-bound squad.

But it was Fortescue, formed after the Australian energy group bought out Penske Autosport's entry and installed Jim Wright as team principal, that won the fight for his signature.

Ticktum explained that the groundwork was laid long before the team's late-season formation, through a conversation with Ekerold, Jaguar race director and Fortescue Zero manager.

“I think it was quite well documented that I was in the frame to be in the Porsche second team [Fusion] for quite some time, and that all became quite tricky and complicated," Ticktum told RacingNews365 during an interview.

"I was told things, and then told other things, and all the rest of it. I actually had, nobody really knew, and this team obviously did come about very late, but I had a very good meeting with Gary a couple of months prior to the London race, at the MotoGP, and he went out of his way to give me an opportunity to speak to him and explain, you know, what has gone wrong in my career, why I am like I am, why Dan Ticktum is who I am, basically.

"And I think he came away from that meeting probably thinking slightly differently,” Ticktum told RacingNews365.

Dan Ticktum pleasantly surprised by Lola GEN4 performance

The Briton said that conversation changed how he viewed his own prospects well before Fortescue existed as a race team.

"I say to you a lot that I feel I've been misunderstood a lot, and I appreciated him giving me the opportunity to speak freely to him with nobody around," continued Ticktum. "So, I mean, I almost wanted to work for him after that, to be honest.

"So then, obviously, the Fortescue deal came about, and I, of course, knew that there would potentially be seats, so I was on the phone very quickly. He [Gary] appointed Jim, and it was my job to obviously convince them that they'd get the right Dan at all times, basically.

"It wasn't about selling them. Some of the things I was saying, I truly meant, and I believe that, having been given this opportunity, it's such a breath of fresh air for me. And, you know, to have a team of this size put their faith in me means that all the people who normally slag me off and say whatever, I don't need to justify myself to them anymore."

As mentioned, in addition to speaking to the new Porsche customer outfit, he also had a solid offer on the table from Lola, who recently announced Robert Shwartzman for the 2027 season.

Ticktum was pleasantly surprised at the performance of Lola's Gen4 car during his tests with the team, and is confident there is no "bad feelings" after choosing Fortescue over them.

"The tests went well," revealed Ticktum. "Yeah, the car was nice to drive actually, very nice to drive. They were figuring out reliability stuff as most teams were over the off-season. But yeah, I think it was useful for them and useful for me.

"So even though I didn't end up there, I don't think there's any bad feelings there at all. But I mean, when I heard that this was coming about, this quite quickly became my number one choice."

title: Toto Wolff discloses 'long-term vision' for Mercedes' F1 success
excerpt:
Toto Wolff has outlined his long-term vision for Mercedes' F1 success, explaining why fostering a safe working environment rather than a "hire-and-fire" culture has been fundamental to the team's return to championship-winning form.

Mercedes has sealed a ninth constructors' title, while Kimi Antonelli has won the drivers' crown in his second season, completing a double that ends four years without a championship for the Brackley-based squad.

The revival follows a difficult stretch from 2022 to 2025, when Mercedes collected only seven grand prix victories after securing eight successive constructors' championships between 2014 and 2021.

George Russell recently praised Wolff's leadership, pointing out that Mercedes had kept faith with the staff responsible for its earlier dominance instead of repeatedly replacing personnel during its struggles.

Asked about Russell's comments, Wolff stressed that the team's approach extended beyond retaining established employees.

"Stability is certainly a factor, but we have also many people who have joined us recently," Wolff told media, including RacingNews365. "And I think what I would like to choose as a word is 'safety'.

"We are not a hire-and-fire organisation. We provide a culture and an environment where you can thrive, where you're allowed to make mistakes, where you can speak up.

"And over the long term, I believe if you want to be successful, not over a period of a few years, but over many, many decades, this is what you need to be able to ingrain in the team, and we're trying that."

[Article continues below]

Key philosophy for 'long-term' success

For Wolff, that philosophy is not simply an explanation for Mercedes' resurgence in 2026.

It is intended to protect the team's competitiveness long after its current championship-winning campaign.

"It's not something you put on a PowerPoint; you have to live those standards day in and day out, and that's what we are... these are the standards we're setting for ourselves," he added.

"Sometimes we fail, but we look at the long-term vision. For me, soon is in 10 years, and I need to set the team up for soon."

title: McLaren face risky dilemma over impending change to F1 rules
excerpt:
Lando Norris' victory at the São Paulo Grand Prix has underlined just how competitive the McLaren can be on a circuit as particular as Interlagos.

The layout mixes a series of medium-speed corners with the long start-finish straight, and it was the former that played to the MCL40's strengths.

That reduced the emphasis on straight-line speed, an area where McLaren's car is notoriously draggy, in the overall lap time.

With a fresh set of parts introduced in Brazil, McLaren has effectively brought forward part of the conceptual shift it is planning for its 2027 car.

A new front wing, new rear wing, new beam wing and an updated floor all arrived at Interlagos.

The aim was to generate more downforce while improving how it is distributed across the car, in pursuit of a better overall balance.

That balance is likely to have made the biggest difference in Brazil, on top of the MCL40's already obvious agility, a product of its extremely short wheelbase.

That wheelbase, however, is set to be lengthened under the 2027 regulations.

It is therefore interesting to consider that elements of this latest upgrade package could carry over to the new car, even though the 2027 concept will be built around a wheelbase roughly 15cm longer.

That change alone will significantly alter load distribution, meaning the aerodynamic maps will look very different from those of the current car.

title: Charles Leclerc avoids thorny Lewis Hamilton question after eye-catching claim
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has avoided answering a thorny question about Lewis Hamilton's claim that the Monegasque races him "differently."

The bubbling tension between the Ferrari drivers erupted on the first lap of the recent Mexico City Grand Prix when Leclerc attacked Hamilton for the lead at Turn 4, with both drivers going off-track.

Leclerc did take first place, but could not cede position to Hamilton as Max Verstappen had squeezed past the #44 Ferrari, with the stewards deciding to hand Leclerc a five-second time penalty.

Ultimately, after a red flag and safety car period, Verstappen beat Hamilton by less than a second, with Leclerc fourth, as the seven-time champion claimed post-race that he was "really pi**ed" at losing a one-two finish, that Leclerc had a "do or die attitude", and that he raced him differently compared to other drivers.

Days later, on the Thursday evening in Brazil, the pair held clear-the-air talks with Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur, who had accused both of disrespecting the Ferrari brand following the contretemps.

Leclerc, who did not hold his traditional Thursday media session after travelling late following the birth of his first child, then fielded questions, at length, for the first time later in the weekend.

He was asked if he agreed with Hamilton's claim that he raced the Briton "differently", to which Leclerc declined to answer.

"I wouldn't want to comment on that," Leclerc straight-batted back to media, including RacingNews365.

"Honestly, there have been way too many comments, and much too much fuss about it for way too long, so I don't really want to get into this kind of comments."

When then asked if he believed that the story had become bigger than it should have, Leclerc agreed.

"I do believe that it stayed much longer than it should have," he said.

[Article continues below]

Leclerc addresses Ferrari battle

It was also put to Leclerc that clashes between two number one drivers were common at top teams, with Hamilton having previous experience between 2013 and 2016 when battling with Nico Rosberg.

It was an assessment Leclerc agreed with.

"I mean, history speaks for itself, and maybe, yeah, looking back, it is maybe something needed," he said.

"At the same time, sometimes you disagree, but you've got to find common ground."

title: Max Verstappen reveals key Red Bull factor in facing major Las Vegas issue
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has flagged tyre warm-up in the Las Vegas cold as the decisive factor for Red Bull heading into next weekend's grand prix.

With track temperatures expected to sit between 10 and 12 degrees Celsius across the sessions over the three days, it makes Las Vegas one of the most unpredictable rounds of the season for tyre behaviour.

The smooth street surface tends to induce sliding, leading to graining and uneven core temperatures rather than the heat build-up drivers get on grippier circuits.

Verstappen, who won last year's race from second on the grid, is wary of reading too much into that result given how differently cars can behave from one Las Vegas weekend to the next.

Asked whether Red Bull would be the team to beat in Las Vegas, the four-time F1 champion was blunt about the unknowns.

"I have no idea because Vegas is so different and so difficult for everyone to understand," he said.

[Article continues below]

Verstappen - 'That's the game this year'

Verstappen also pointed to the circuit's long straight as a separate challenge, one tied to this year's energy deployment rules rather than temperature.

"First of all, deployment," he remarked. "It's a very long straight, so I think I would need to tuck in in the middle of the straight to try and gain some top speed. That is just the game this year.

"With energy management on that straight, it's going to be very, very difficult.

"Actually, maybe the track will be a bit like Monza, where slipstreaming each other is quite good, quite beneficial.

"But the problem is that it's so cold over there that you get very different behaviour from every car. Some suddenly work extremely well on a track like that. We've seen it in the past."

Red Bull has traditionally struggled to a degree on low-grip, cold-track layouts where downforce loading builds less aggressively than through high-speed corners, in contrast to its usual strength in preserving tyres in hotter conditions.

Verstappen made clear he sees that as the team's biggest obstacle again this year.

"I have to say that it's normally not our best track because of that", he said.

"But we'll see if we can get the tyres to work. That's the key, to be honest, around there."

title: Lewis Hamilton lambasts F1 peers for 'talking smack' and lacking empathy
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has scolded certain former F1 drivers and even some of his peers still racing in the championship for "talking smack" about younger drivers still establishing themselves.

Hamilton expressed his pride in the crop of young drivers breaking through for how they handle the trials and tribulations that come with racing in the most visible form of motorsport in the world, calling out those who have "no empathy" despite having shared that same experience.

It is a subject the seven-time F1 drivers' champion feels passionately about, and it is something he has addressed before.

When Hamilton emerged almost two decades ago, many former drivers were hard on him, a practice that has continued to this day, with pundits routinely outspoken about his performance and career.

In the wake of Kimi Antonelli winning his first F1 title at just 20 years of age, the Ferrari driver was asked for his feelings about witnessing the next generation make their mark.

"It doesn't make me reflect on my career; I think I'm just really proud to see new people coming through, young drivers," Hamilton told media, including RacingNews365, before taking the opportunity to send a clear message.

"I see a lot of these ex-Formula 1 drivers, or older Formula 1 drivers, racing drivers, just talking smack about young people all the time.

"And even though they have gone through something similar, they just have no empathy, and I always wanted to make sure that I would not be that type of driver.

"So I always want to praise for what's deserved, and it's been amazing to see that all these young drivers, even further down the grid and in the other teams, they're all showing up every single week with all the pressures that they have."

[Article continues below]

Hamilton: 'I really respect' their tenacity and resilience

Following the packed rookie class of 2025, there is a good mix of young and experienced drivers currently racing in F1.

Hamilton voiced his respect for the cohort of drivers that, in addition to Antonelli, includes Oliver Bearman, Gabriel Bortoleto, Isack Hadjar and Franco Colapinto, who have since been joined by Arvid Lindblad and Rafael Camara.

"Of course, we're very, very privileged as racing drivers, but there are massive challenges to arrive and keep your head up and keep failing and getting back up, and they're all doing that with real humility and grace, I think," Hamilton added.

"And, of course, they're making mistakes along the way, but this is the pinnacle of motorsport.

"It is the hardest platform to do well, and it's so easy to make mistakes. The easiest is to drop the ball, but I can understand how it is for each of them just getting up and picking up and just continuing to push. So I really respect that."

title: Daniel Ricciardo explains 'shoey' origin: 'I felt like a tie was choking everyone'
excerpt:
Daniel Ricciardo has revealed that the celebration that came to define his F1 career began as a message to friends back home in Australia rather than a calculated stunt.

Ricciardo, who retired from Formula 1 after the 2024 Singapore Grand Prix following 257 starts, eight wins and 32 podiums across a 14-year career, has reflected on the gesture that followed him from Red Bull to Renault, and onto McLaren.

Ricciardo said the act began on the podium after the 2016 German Grand Prix, in which he was second, long before it became an expected ritual whenever he finished on the rostrum.

"I did it really for my friends watching back home, and I knew that they'd text me after being like, 'You're a legend. You did it for Australia'," said Ricciardo. "[I was a] Bit of a bogan, someone who doesn't take themselves so seriously, I guess.

"And there were some friends and a group of guys in Australia who were doing a lot of it, and they had quite a big presence on social media and stuff.

"So it was becoming like Australia, or a part of Australia, was owning it a little bit, and then there were some Australian sports people and celebrities and that who were doing it.

"So I was like, 'Okay, I want to be a part of this and show Australia that I'm proud to be Australian."

[Article continues below]

Riccaiardo - 'Let's undo a button'

Ricciardo explained that beyond the Australian pride angle, he also wanted to loosen up a paddock he found overly formal, even in victory.

"There was definitely a conscious part of it, where the sport was still very serious," he said. "I would see drivers on the podium sometimes, and they looked miserable, and I couldn't really understand why.

"I get it if you lose the race on the last lap and you finish second instead of first.

"But there were a lot of situations where I was like, the sport feels a little stiff, and that was also my way of trying to bring in something else to the sport. I felt like the tie was choking everyone, and I was like, 'Let's undo a button here and relax a little'.

"And then it just became my thing, and it wasn't really planned to have been something that I would have done again."

It became such an iconic moment on the podium that others followed suit, not least the late renowned actor Sir Patrick Stewart after the 2017 Canadian GP.

"I hadn't even got to the point of asking him if he wanted to do it yet," said Ricciardo. "He asked me if he could do it, so he basically demanded it, and I was like, 'This is very cool', so I knew it had caught some wind by that point."

Even seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton got in on the act, after previously stating that, "The juice from the foot is not something I wish to drink."

Ricciardo said: "Lewis was also quoted saying once he'd never do it, and then he did.

"I'm just glad it was always my shoe. I gave the people what they wanted."

title: Alan Jones remembered for 'indelible mark' in touching Williams family tribute
excerpt:
Alan Jones left an "indelible mark" on the history of the Williams F1 team, believes former boss Claire Williams.

Jones, the 1980 F1 world champion, died last week aged 80 after a short illness in Australia.

The 12-time grand prix winner entered the history books in 1980 as the first driver to win the world title for Williams, with the likes of Nelson Piquet, Nigel Mansell, and Alain Prost following in his footsteps for Sir Frank Williams and Sir Patrick Head.

Jones was often used as the yardstick by which all Williams drivers were judged, having raced for the team between 1978 and 1981, with former deputy team principal and Sir Frank's daughter, Claire, reflecting on the Melbourne native's passing.

"It was so sad to hear of Alan's passing," Williams told RacingNews365 exclusively.

"There are a number of people who have been a part of the team over a long, long period of our history, and there have been a good handful that have left such an indelible mark as Alan did.

"He was Dad and Patrick's first world champion, and that meant an enormous amount. I was very young; I was only four when Alan raced for us, but I knew him and built a lovely relationship with him when I was team principal, and he was enormously supportive of me, courtesy of his relationship with my dad.

"He wasn't a driver that came and went as much as his time in the sport was pretty short comparatively. He just had a personality that my dad truly admired and respected, and I think they were very similar in their personalities.

"It was that just kind of mindset of roll your sleeves up, put in every ounce of your fibre to get the job done and to win. That was their mindset.

"Unfortunately, it's another racing great [who has died]. It's another icon who is no longer here, and that's incredibly sad.

"My thoughts are with his family, with his friends, and those who will feel his passing sorely."

title: Isack Hadjar expresses sadness at all-too-soon F1 season ending
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar has expressed his sadness that the F1 season is on the cusp of ending, declaring that he still feels like he has "a lot in the tank."

In his first season at Red Bull, Hadjar has performed well, scooping three podiums in support of Max Verstappen, but missed the Dutch, Italian, and Spanish Grands Prix after sustaining a wrist injury during the summer break, meaning he did not race between the Hungarian GP on July 26th and the Azerbaijan GP on September 26th.

This two-month lay-off came after no grands prix were held in April, with the Bahrain and Saudi Arabian races unable to be held as scheduled due to the Iran War, with one race in the two months between the Japanese GP on March 29th and the Canadian GP on May 26th.

Although F1 has signalled that the Qatar and Abu Dhabi races will go ahead to finish the season with Imola formally stood down as a replacement venue, there is a slim possibility that the upcoming Las Vegas GP could still be the end of the campaign if tensions in the Middle East re-escalate.

Reflecting on whether his injury lay-off had disrupted his momentum, Hadjar rejected the idea.

"No, because I got very lucky with the timing because the three races I skipped, I remember, were a bit tricky," Hadjar told media, including RacingNews365.

"I definitely came back when the car made the step. At the same time, I feel like this year, for some reason, I feel like I haven't driven much.

"Bahrain and Saudi Arabia were cancelled, and then I had a two-month break during the summer, and now I feel like I have a lot left in the tank, and considering what's happening in the coming races and we don't know how many more races we are going to have, I'm a bit sad that we're already at the end.

"I feel like I can still go a long way this year."

[Article continues below]

Red Bull's step forward

Since Hadjar returned to Baku, the team has enjoyed a strong run of form, with Verstappen winning three races in Bahrain, Malaysia, Singapore, and Mexico City, as well as the Singapore Sprint.

Hadjar has taken podiums in Baku and Sao Paulo in addition to his one earlier in the season in Monaco, just as the RB22 has taken a dramatic upturn in performance - something he says gives him hope for 2027.

"But I'm proud of the guys for the big step [we made]," he said.

"In Melbourne we were second off the pace; at round three [in Japan], we were a second off. Now the car is winning races and fighting for podiums, so I can't be more proud of that.

"The way we developed the car, the ability of the team to progress quickly [makes me] very hopeful for next year."
